3.0.s.en: (1) The multitude of those who trouble him

3.0.0.en: 1- Lord, how are they increased that trouble me! many are they that rise up against me.

3.0.1.en: 1- While David was fleeing in great humiliation from the face of his son Absalom, running barefoot with his head covered and weeping, he felt very deep sorrow, and wrote this lament.

3.0.2.en: 2- And the beautiful thing is that in his great distress he did not grieve privately within himself, but took refuge in God in a humble prayer, in which he declares his weakness and the multitude of those who trouble and oppose him, because Absalom gathered behind him a great army, indeed all the Jewish people, not only to drive David out of his kingdom but trying to kill him.

3.0.3.en: 3- Although God had foretold David what would happen (2 Sam 12:11) through the mouth of Nathan the prophet after his fall into adultery, David did not despair or surrender to evil, but raised his voice in faith toward God to rescue him from those who opposed him, and He had compassion on him and saved him.

3.0.4.en: 4- And David here is a type of Christ, that is, this Psalm, as we said, speaks about the feelings of Christ when the Jews arrested Him, tortured Him and crucified Him, and the likeness between David and Christ in this situation appears in the following:

3.0.5.en: a- His son Absalom rose up against David, and the Jewish nation, His daughter, rose up against Christ to kill Him.

3.0.6.en: b- David's friend and counselor Ahithophel betrayed him, and afterwards hanged himself. And Christ was betrayed by His friend and disciple Judas Iscariot, who then hanged himself.

3.0.7.en: c- David had compassion on his rebellious son Absalom and charged his army to deal gently with him. And Christ had compassion on those who crucified Him and prayed for them on the Cross, saying, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 23:34).

3.0.8.en: d- All the tribes of the children of Israel rose up against David. And all the Jews rose up against Christ to be rid of Him.

3.1.0.en: 2- Many there be which say of my soul, There is no help for him in God. Selah.

3.1.1.en: 1- When many people gathered behind Absalom and David fled before them, they said to him that he has no salvation in his God, because he had few with him, while Absalom had a great army with him. They forgot that power belongs to God and not to a great number. David, who was wronged, must be defended by God, and although He allowed this tribulation as discipline for him for his sin, He is merciful and accepts the repentance of His children and saves them if the wicked wrong them.

3.1.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who was wronged like David, and the Jews said about Him, "let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him" (Mt 27:42). This verse applies to all God's children when they pass through tribulation and Satan tries to make them fall into despair, which is the hardest sin, but by their supplications they receive deliverance and victory from God. Satan may fight man with despair through the words of people, as Job's wife said to him (Job 2:9) and as Tobit's relatives said to him (Tob 2:16). Satan may also fight man with inner thoughts, but in every case by returning to God man finds his hope and strength.

3.1.3.en: 3- After this verse there is the word Selah, which is a musical pause to give man an opportunity to reflect on the preceding words, that is, how hard the tribulation is and the doubts cast by human beings, so that this drives him to take refuge in God. The word Selah will come twice more in this Psalm (vv. 4, 8) for the same purpose.

3.1.4.en: Hasten to God in all your needs and tribulations, confident that He is very near to you and ready to keep you however much evils surround you. Do not believe thoughts of doubt and despair however logical they seem, for they are the lying words of Satan, because he tries to make you forget the power of God that is with you.

3.2.0.en: 3- But thou, O Lord, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head.

3.2.1.en: Shield: a defensive instrument in war, consisting of a piece of wood covered with leather and having a handle at the back, into which the warrior puts his hand, so that by moving his hand he can protect his head and body from the enemy's arrows.

3.2.2.en: 1- David answered the doubts of his enemies by taking refuge in God, that is, he did not speak with them, because their speech is the speech of Satan, but spoke with God and said to Him, You are my shield, that is, my protection and my fortress, however much the enemies surround me, and You will also do a positive work with me, which is that You will glorify me and lift up my head. And this is what actually happened, for when Absalom dared to attack David, his army was broken and he died, and David returned with great honor to his throne.

3.2.3.en: 2- The shield is the shield of faith (Eph 6:16); by faith David prayed to God, confident that He protects him from Absalom and those with him.

3.2.4.en: 3- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, for the Son says to the Father, You are my shield and my protection, however much the wicked try to ensnare me in a word, or kill me, and after this You glorify me by the Cross, by which I accomplish salvation and redemption for mankind, and by my death I lift the sentence of death from those who believe in me, and then You lift up my head by the resurrection from the dead.

3.3.0.en: 4- I cried unto the Lord with my voice, and he heard me out of his holy hill. Selah.

3.3.1.en: His holy hill: His temple, or the heaven of heavens, the place of His dwelling.

3.3.2.en: 1- When David was driven out of Jerusalem, far from God's temple set on a hill, he was not troubled, because he was confident that his prayers and his cry toward God's hill would be answered by God and He would keep him, and even bring him back to his kingdom.

3.3.3.en: 2- This verse, as a prophecy about Christ, means that the Psalmist, like every believer, cries out to Christ crucified on the hill of Golgotha, and He answers him and grants him salvation, and Christ is symbolized by the hill, as Daniel said that he saw a stone cut out without hands and it became a mountain (Dan 2:34, 35).

3.3.4.en: 3- And we cry out in all our petitions to the Father through His Son Jesus Christ the Redeemer, crucified on the hill, in whom we trust, and He saves us from all our distresses.

3.3.5.en: 4- And Christ cried out on the Cross and gave up the spirit, and God answered Him and raised Him from the dead on the third day.

3.3.6.en: 5- Crying out is not only outward with the mouth, but can also be inward, as Moses cried out within himself and no one heard him except God, who said to him, "Wherefore criest thou unto me?" (Ex 14:15).

3.3.7.en: 6- This verse carries the meanings of prayer, faith in God, His love and His answering us; therefore we find at its end the word Selah, to give man an opportunity to reflect on all this.

3.4.0.en: 5- I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the Lord sustained me. 6- I will not be afraid of ten thousands of people, that have set themselves against me round about.

3.4.1.en: 1- David felt that through his negligence he had lain down and slept in sin, when he sinned with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, but through repentance God removes his sin from him and raises him from it, and he awakes and returns to his sonship to God.

3.4.2.en: 2- It is a clear prophecy about Christ, who lay down on the Cross and slept, that is, died, and by His lying down and His death gave rest and salvation to all who believe in Him, because sleep gives man rest. Christ died, and in Him we all died, to receive salvation with Him, as our teacher Paul the Apostle says, "For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God" (Col 3:3). Then He awoke, that is, rose from the dead on the third day, to raise us in Him. So the believer does not despair if he falls into any sin and lies down in it, but believes that through repentance he receives justification from it and rises with Christ, to begin a new life in Him.

3.4.3.en: 3- These words show the extent of the peace of heart: despite the severe tribulation and his exposure to death, he lay down and slept in God's hands, confident of His care, and then awoke in the morning, because the hand of the Lord upholds and sustains him, and he feels secure, whether in his palace inside Jerusalem or in the wilderness while pursued by Absalom. Consequently he does not fear the tens of thousands who follow Absalom from the people of the children of Israel, who have risen up against him to kill him; however ready and arrayed they are to fight him, with many weapons, all this is worth nothing so long as God protects him.

3.4.4.en: Remind yourself of God who is with you, by repeating prayers, to keep a calm heart, whatever problems surround you, because God is the one who protects you from them.

3.5.0.en: 7- Arise, O Lord; save me, O my God: for thou hast smitten all mine enemies upon the cheek bone; thou hast broken the teeth of the ungodly.

3.5.1.en: 1- Although David is reassured of God's support, he sees the multitude of the enemies and their strength; therefore he asks God, who has been long-suffering toward Absalom, to arise now to stop their attack, which has come near him. And he asks God to save him from the hands of his enemies, that is, to complete his salvation and keep them away from him. He trusts in God's power, so he asks Him to arise and stop the evil.

3.5.2.en: 2- And David remembers the power of God, which formerly struck his enemies and all who tried to kill him, namely Saul and all who followed him, and God struck them on the jaw and shattered and broke their teeth, that is, removed their strength, and this means:

3.5.3.en: a- Their evil speech that they utter from their mouths against him.

3.5.4.en: b- Their strength, which is represented by their teeth, which want to devour him, but God shatters and breaks them, so they become worthless.

3.5.5.en: c- The jaw and teeth signify the power of those around Christ who persecuted Him and crucified Him, but they could not prevent His power, which bound Satan, and then His resurrection from the dead.

3.5.6.en: d- The jaw and teeth signify the innovations and heresies and blasphemies against the Holy Spirit that fought the Church, but God shattered them and stopped them by His power in the ecumenical councils and by the power of His holy children.

3.5.7.en: e- The jaw and teeth also signify the power of the demons that surround God's children in every generation, and God rescues His children from them.

3.5.8.en: 3- God strikes the enemies on the jaw, that perhaps they may repent, but if they persist in their evil, He protects His children and His Church by shattering their teeth, that is, He deprives them of their strength with which they harm God's children.

3.6.0.en: 8- Salvation belongeth unto the Lord: thy blessing is upon thy people. Selah.

3.6.1.en: 1- In the end David declares that salvation is from God alone and not from human power, so that no one depends on his own abilities or relationships, for no one will save him from evil except God.

3.6.2.en: 2- He also affirms that God blesses His people and His children, and so long as God blesses them no one can harm them.

3.6.3.en: 3- David asks salvation for himself from God, and also salvation and blessing for his people, whom Absalom led into the way of evil, for God is able to restore them to their peace and their life with Him. And this is what actually happened, for Absalom was killed in the war, and the people returned to God and submitted to David and restored him to his throne.

3.6.4.en: 4- David ascribes the people to God, saying "thy people"; for he humbly sees himself as merely a small instrument in God's hand, and it is God who set him as king over this people, so he asks God with boldness to bless His people who belong to Him and to save David by His power, so that he may return to lead God's people.

3.6.5.en: 5- "Selah", as we said, represents a musical pause, and it is an opportunity to reflect on the Lord who saves His children.

3.6.6.en: 6- Thus we see that this Psalm begins with distress and ends with salvation; therefore the one who prays sings it at the beginning of the day, so that he is not troubled by any problems that may meet him this day, or those that are still with him from previous days, for God is able to save him from them and in the midst of them. This Psalm is also said at the end of the prayers of Great Friday, after Christ bore all our sufferings on the Cross, but by His death He saves us from all our sins.

3.6.7.en: Ask God with faith and be persistent with Him, for He is able to save you, and even to bless you, so that you lift up your heart in thanksgiving to Him always.

3.6.8.en: The life of righteousness To the chief Musician on Neginoth, A Psalm of David. "Hear me when I call" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

3.6.9.en: 1- Its writer: the prophet David, as is stated in the title.

3.6.10.en: 2- We find a title for this Psalm that it is for the chief Musician, that is, it was sung by a large company of singers having a leader or conductor, so it is a Psalm for the people, sung before a large assembly, and this shows its importance.

3.6.11.en: 3- We also find in its title that it is "on Neginoth", that is, it was sung to the accompaniment of an ancient stringed musical instrument called Neginoth, that is, having a number of strings.

3.6.12.en: 4- In the Septuagint we find in its title "Unto the end, a Psalm of David."

3.6.13.en: The meaning of "unto the end" is as follows:

3.6.14.en: a- In (v. 1) he says "God of my righteousness", that is, God is the source of my righteousness, and "unto the end" means unto Christ, who became incarnate and in whom the righteousness of God appeared, and who is also the one who in the end reigns forever over the hearts of all who believe in Him, who sang and prayed to Him in their life on earth, so they deserve to sing with Him a new song in heaven forever.

3.6.15.en: b- Unto the end, that is, he sings throughout his life, because of the importance of the Psalm.

3.6.16.en: c- The end is David's victory over all his enemies surrounding his country and his subduing them to himself, and by this he is a type of Christ, who in the end subjects all His enemies, the demons, to Himself, for He bound them on the Cross, and at the end of days He casts them into eternal torment, declaring the victory of His children over them and glorifying them in heaven with Him.

3.6.17.en: 5- The Fathers see that there is a connection between the third and fourth Psalms, for David feels sorrow in both; if the third Psalm is a lament of David when Absalom rose up against him, the fourth Psalm is an extension of it, because he says in it "How long shall my glory be turned into shame?" and "how long will ye love vanity, and seek after leasing?" (v. 2).

3.6.18.en: 6- Some of the Fathers see that David said this Psalm during Saul's pursuit of him, when Michal helped him to escape (1 Sam 19:11-12), and God delivered him from the hand of Saul, so David thanks God, the God of his righteousness.
